summary:
Groundstory is an interactive site that puts NISAR radar measurements of ground change next to sourced accounts from the places affected, plus the repeatable scalable open-source pipeline for people to build their own.

For twelve events from 2026 (four earthquakes, three eruptions, a sinking city, a debris flow, a flood and two wildfires) it shows the terrain in 3D with the NISAR change layer on it, a before/after slider, and pins on named places: a school, a shrine, a bridge. Each pin carries what a field survey or news report recorded there and what NISAR measured at that spot.

Radar maps are hard for non-specialists to read. Our hypothesis is that a measurement means more beside a place people recognise or a human story. We also show where radar falls short, because an honest picture of what it cannot see is part of understanding it.
details:
What it does

  • Explore. The site opens on the Kumamoto earthquake of 28 July 2026. You see the terrain in 3D, a Sentinel-2 image from before and after, and the NISAR layer showing how far the ground moved toward or away from the satellite. Pins mark places with a sourced account, each with its photo, credit and the radar reading at that point. Eleven more events (fires, eruptions, floods, quakes) use the same page. Every event gets its own bespoke end-to-end explanation of the science behind how the visualization was created.
  • Create. A step-by-step guide takes a developer from an event name to a finished page, including when to stop because the coverage or the signal isn't good enough.

How it works

We researched 21 candidate events across different types (fire, quake, flood, subsidence, eruption etc.). However anyone can use the same pipeline to build a groundstory for their own chosen events.

  1. Check coverage. A search of NASA's catalogue (CMR) keeps events with NISAR passes before and after.
  2. Read only what is needed. NISAR files are 1 to 5 GB. The pipeline reads just the window around the event: 54 MB for Kumamoto, not about 4 GB.
  3. Clean the measurement. For ground motion (NISAR GUNW) we remove the ionosphere estimate, drop low-coherence pixels, keep the largest reliably unwrapped region and measure against the window's median. A quiet pair from before the event shows what noise looks like on the same ground: at Kumamoto the motion range is 30.7 cm across the earthquake and 6.9 cm in the quiet pair. Fires and floods use the change in radar brightness (NISAR GCOV).
  4. Add context. Copernicus terrain and Sentinel-2 imagery are put on the same grid as the radar.
  5. Place the stories. Each account is checked on its source page, located, given a confidence level and a recorded licence, then sampled against the radar. A person, not the pipeline, chooses what is published. Ten events carry 58 located stories.
  6. Visualize and publish.

What we found

  • The idea works best where the event leaves a sharp edge in the ground: a fault rupture, the rim of a sinking basin, a lava front.
  • It is weak for fires, floods and debris flows. Radar brightness picks out only part of a burn, flood water can drain between passes, and the pixels are coarser than a debris channel. The pages say so.
  • One radar view measures one direction. At Kumamoto the plain beside the fault reads "closer to the satellite", yet GPS shows it slid 87 cm north-east and sank 32 cm. A prototype view slides the two sides of the fault using field-survey and GPS data, labelled as not measured by NISAR. Measuring that sideways motion from the radar itself is the next step.
  • At Anak Krakatau, NISAR radar brightness shows about 26 hectares of new land appearing with the September eruption, seen from two directions and matched by optical imagery. This appears to confirm Indonesia's geological agency reported 32.8 hectares (though the two small islets it also reported do not show).
  • It's hard to find good media with permissive rights. AI/SI can help build tooling but final selection of high-quality media has to be done by people.

Benefits and intended impact

The audience is the public, teachers and journalists: people who see a radar map after a disaster and can't tell what it means for a place they know. We have not yet tested with users whether the stories improve understanding; a small comprehension test is the first thing we would do next. The pipeline is the second benefit: anyone can build a page for a new event.

Tools

  • Data: NISAR L2 GUNW and GCOV (provisional) from the ASF DAAC, found through NASA CMR with Earthdata Login; Copernicus Sentinel-2 and GLO-30 terrain; OpenStreetMap.
  • Pipeline: Python 3.12 with NumPy, SciPy, h5py, rasterio, pyproj, Pillow and Requests; tests in pytest.
  • Site: static HTML, CSS and JavaScript with three.js, hosted on GitHub Pages. No server and no special hardware.
  • AI: AI models and coding agents did research, wrote most of the code and drafted the docs. Every value and source was checked against the original. No image, video or map on the site is AI-generated.

How it is creative

Most radar visualisations start from orbit and stop at the map. We start from a place on the ground and pull back to the measurement, so the schoolyard and the radar pattern appear in the same view. The editor that lets a person choose and caption the stories is part of the product. We also tried a paper-map style with a "cut" tool that plots the radar reading along a line you draw; it stayed an experiment.

What we considered

  • What the radar can and can't say. Motion is along the satellite's line of sight, not up and down. Lost coherence doesn't prove damage. A story near a boundary doesn't prove the boundary caused it. NISAR data are provisional.
    (We attempted to infer quake slip from radar alone, and then in tandem with GPS measurements - this remains future work.)
  • Keeping sources apart. Field-survey numbers, GPS and radar readings are labelled separately.
  • Rights. Every photo carries its credit and licence. News images appear only as pixelated previews linked to the article.
  • Openness. Code and text are CC0, and a test fails if the credits fall out of date.
